title: KYC needed to be resumable without making people start over

children.text: The earlier KYC flow followed one fixed sequence. Users completed KTP first, then Selfie, before moving into identity details and submission.
Autosave made that structure worth revisiting. Saving progress had limited value if users still had to follow the same order or repeat work after leaving the flow.
I designed two flow directions, set up the usability study, analyzed the behavioral and survey evidence, then translated the decision into product rules for implementation.

callout: Autosave became more useful once saved progress changed how the flow itself behaved.

title: We tested a fixed sequence against a flexible task hub
description: Both concepts saved progress. The difference was how much the surrounding KYC structure changed once that progress could persist.

left.label: Flow A
left.title: Keep the existing sequence
left.description: Users followed the predetermined order and the guide remained a required step before moving to the next task.
left.alt: Flow A KYC with a fixed sequence
left.note: Autosave sits inside the old interaction pattern.

right.label: Flow B
right.title: Turn Review into a task hub
right.description: Users see the status of KTP and Selfie in one place, choose where to start, and return to the hub after completing one task.
right.alt: Flow B KYC with Review as a task hub
right.note: Autosave changes the interaction structure as well as persistence.

title: The extra flexibility needed testing because it also introduced more choice

children.text: Flow B gave users more control and made progress easier to inspect. It also added a decision that did not exist in the earlier sequence.
I wanted to check whether that tradeoff made KYC harder to understand. Both directions were therefore tested as end-to-end experiences rather than compared only as wireframes.

title: The study did not produce a statistical winner

children.text: SUS and total misclicks showed no significant difference between Flow A and Flow B. Several perception measures followed the same pattern.

I then looked at the descriptive data and open feedback without treating them as inferential proof. Flow B showed a lower misclick trend, steadier confidence, and feedback that was more supportive of the progress hub.
Flow B also matched the product model better because each task was already meant to persist independently. There was no meaningful usability penalty that justified keeping the older sequence.

callout: Flow B gave us enough confidence to move forward while staying within what the study actually supported.

title: The product decision stayed separate from the statistical claim
description: The study informed the direction, but it did not justify saying that Flow B was statistically proven to be better.

left.label: Not supported
left.title: Flow B won the A B test
left.description: There was no significant difference in SUS or total misclicks, so the study did not establish a statistical winner.

right.label: Supported for the decision
right.title: Flow B was a reasonable production baseline
right.description: Usability did not meaningfully deteriorate, while the behavioral trend, feedback, and Autosave model all supported the more flexible structure.
right.note: Decision confidence came from the full body of evidence.

title: A non-significant study can still support a strong product decision

children.text: The study did not produce a statistical winner. That made the decision boundary clearer. Flow B could move forward because usability did not meaningfully deteriorate and its behavior matched what Autosave needed to support.

A next iteration should measure resume rate, retakes by task, and completion after users return. Those measures would make the value of persistence easier to separate from other KYC changes happening around it.
